summary: An informational discussion of the issues that arise for network-layer routing, especially unicast routing, when the Internet is run by many competing providers rather than a single backbone. It lays out the problems and considerations rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1787 looks at what happens to Internet routing when many companies each run part of the network. It lists the problems that creates, from who pays for extra routing information to what happens when a customer changes provider, and closes with a list of work for the community to do.

questions: how does routing work with multiple internet providers
what are the problems of multi-provider routing
why is renumbering needed with cidr
what are source and destination routing preferences
who pays for extra routing information
subtitle: An IAB discussion of what happens to Internet routing when many competing providers run the network.

tldr.problem: The Internet was no longer run by a single backbone but by many providers with different and sometimes conflicting goals, and with no central control, while Internet-wide connectivity still needed cooperative routing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines no protocol. It surveys the issues: what routing requirements exist and who should pay for them, encapsulation, price structures, scalability, hierarchical routing and renumbering, and sharing routing information between organisations.
tldr.outcome: It ends with a list of further work, split into immediate, medium term and long term, with easier renumbering and aggregation above the direct provider level named as the most urgent.

today: RFC 1787 is an Informational memo offered by the IAB to stimulate discussion, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol.

sections.title: Network Service Providers and Subscribers
sections.content:
Within the current routing paradigm, the service a provider offers at the network layer, IP, is the set of destinations, meaning hosts, that can be reached through that provider. Once a subscriber establishes direct connectivity to a provider, the subscriber can in principle reach all the destinations reachable through it. Because the value of the Internet-wide connectivity a provider offers increases with the number of destinations reachable through it, providers are motivated to interconnect with each other.

A provider need not offer the same service to all of its subscribers. For some subscribers a provider may restrict the service to a subset of the reachable destinations, and for certain kinds of subscriber constrained connectivity can be part of the service offered.

In a multi-provider environment individual providers may be driven by diverse and sometimes conflicting goals. Some exist to serve only a specific group of subscribers, others place no constraints on subscribers as long as they pay, some constrain the reselling of connectivity by organisations attached to them, and some are operated by companies subject to specific regulations while others are unregulated. The geographical coverage of providers ranges from a county or town to country-wide, international or intercontinental.

There is no centralised control over the providers, they do not always coordinate with each other, and quite often they compete. Despite all this, Internet-wide IP connectivity is realised through Internet-wide distributed routing, which involves multiple providers and therefore implies a degree of cooperation and coordination. The memo says there is a need to balance the providers' goals against the public interest of Internet-wide connectivity and subscribers' choices, and that further work is needed to understand how to reach that balance.
sections.plainLanguage: Many companies run different parts of the network and sometimes compete, but the Internet works only if they cooperate on routing. The memo says the balance between the two is not settled.

sections.title: Routing Requirements and Their Cost
sections.content:
Routing requirements fall into three categories. Source preferences allow the originator of a packet to control the path to a destination. Destination preferences allow a destination to control the path from a source to it. Constraints on transit traffic allow a provider to control the traffic that traverses the routers and links it controls.

The degree of control varies. For source and destination preferences it can range from simply providing connectivity regardless of the path, through selecting immediate providers, to a subscriber wanting complete control over path selection. For transit traffic it can range from control based only on the direct physical connectivity, meaning the set of organisations directly connected to the provider, through restricting traffic to a particular set of sources or destinations, to a combination of both, or even taking account of the paths to and from those sources and destinations.

The memo then asks who pays. A situation where one organisation can unilaterally impose routing information overhead on another, for example by requiring that organisation to maintain extra routing information, is undesirable. The cost of supporting a routing requirement should not be borne by organisations that do not benefit from it, and ideally the routing system should let the overhead move towards whoever caused the requirement. It gives the example of balancing the overhead of maintaining state for multi-hop header compression against carrying explicit forwarding information on a per-packet basis. Organisations with simple requirements should not bear the same overhead as organisations with complex ones. It also notes that a requirement whose overhead has to be carried by every router and host in the organisation imposing it is undesirable, because an organisation should be able to instantiate its requirements in a more or less central fashion, for example by using only some of its routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender, the receiver and the network owner each want a say in the route taken. Whoever asks for special rules should pay for them, and simple users should not carry the cost of complex ones.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Price Structure
sections.content:
Encapsulation creates a virtual IP overlay over an existing IP infrastructure, and that has implications for the routing system. In the presence of encapsulation a provider may no longer be able to constrain its transit traffic to a particular set of ultimate sources or destinations, because a packet may be encapsulated by some router along the path, with the original source and destination addresses hidden at the network layer. Encapsulation may also affect source and destination preferences, because a source or a destination may either be unaware of the encapsulation or have little or no control over the encapsulated segment of a path. The memo says further work is needed to understand the implications of the overlay capabilities created by encapsulation on the semantics of routing requirements, and on the interaction between the entities that form the overlay and those that form the underlying infrastructure.

Price structure also shapes routing. Routing among providers and between providers and subscribers may be influenced by the price structure the providers employ and by the usage pattern of the subscribers. A provider can view routing as a mechanism for controlling who can use its services, and a subscriber as a mechanism for controlling the price it pays for Internet connectivity. The need to exert control has to be balanced against the cost of the routing mechanisms needed to provide it. In a competitive market, the memo says, one could question the viability of a mechanism whose incremental cost would be greater than the saving it recovers, because competitive pressure or alternative mechanisms are likely to push providers and subscribers towards the cheapest mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: If a packet is wrapped inside another one, the network owner cannot see where it is really going, so rules about transit traffic may not work. And whatever control a party wants has to be worth what it costs.

sections.title: Scalability and Aggregation
sections.content:
One of the key requirements on Internet routing is the ability to scale. Beyond the usual measures such as memory, CPU and bandwidth, the memo adds scalability with respect to the human resources needed to operate the system. The need for CIDR already showed that a routing scheme scaling linearly with the number of connected networks, or even with the number of connected organisations, is unacceptable today and likely to be unacceptable in the long term. It is not clear whether routing that scales linearly with the number of providers will be acceptable in the long term.

Scaling implies the routing system needs powerful mechanisms for aggregation and abstraction of routing information. In the absence of Internet-wide coordination and in the presence of competition among providers, those mechanisms should minimise preconditions and limit the amount of inter-provider coordination required. Ideally a provider should be able to control the amount of its own local resources needed to deal with routing overhead based on purely local considerations.

One side effect of aggregation and abstraction is that some routing information is lost, which may affect route optimality and even the ability to find an existing route. Aggregation also implies a certain homogeneity of the information being aggregated, and that has to be counter-balanced against the potential diversity of routing requirements. As a way to deal with the information loss, the memo says we need to explore mechanisms that allow routing based on the on-demand acquisition of subsets of unaggregated information. Finally, the overhead of supporting specific routing requirements has a direct impact on the overall scalability of the routing system, so we need to understand that impact and, when it is significant and the requirement matters in practice, develop mechanisms that reduce it.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing has to keep up with the size of the Internet, not just in memory and processor time but in the people needed to run it. Grouping many routes into one summary keeps the tables small, but loses detail, and the memo asks for ways to get that detail back only when it is needed.

sections.title: Hierarchical Routing and Renumbering
sections.content:
CIDR, specified in RFC 1518 and RFC 1519 and used today for scalable Internet-wide routing, is based on hierarchical routing. Essential to that technique is the assumption that the network layer addresses assigned to individual entities reflect the position of those entities within the network topology; the addresses are said to be topologically significant. With CIDR, the addresses assigned to most sites are expected to reflect the providers those sites connect to, so the addresses are provider-based.

One fundamental consequence is that to preserve the topological significance of addresses, changes in the network topology may need matching changes in addresses. Because multiple providers serve the same geographical area, a subscriber should be able to switch from one provider to another, and since such a switch implies a change in the Internet topology, the subscriber has to change the addresses of all of its entities. That process is called renumbering. Tools already exist to help with it, namely the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, but DHCP is not yet widely deployed, and further work is needed to improve the tools, get them deployed widely and integrate them with the Domain Name System.

Multi-level hierarchical routing allows extra routing information, which the memo calls routing entropy, to be recaptured because of a mismatch between addresses and topology at one level of the hierarchy. This lets the routing system contain the scope of the entities affected by the mismatch, which could be an important factor in graceful renumbering, and deployment strategies for those capabilities need to be developed.

The requirement for topologically significant addresses does not have to be applied to every organisation connected to the Internet. Hierarchical routing needs most, but not all, addresses to be topologically significant. For a large organisation it could be enough for its destinations to appear as a small number of address prefixes even if those prefixes are independent of the providers it uses, that is, provider-independent addresses; the routing information such an organisation injects would then be comparable to the aggregated routing information of a large number of small organisations.

Multiple providers also allow a subscriber to be connected to more than one provider at the same time. CIDR offers several alternatives for handling such multi-homed subscribers, and more operational experience and understanding of the trade-offs is needed. The memo also considers assigning addresses purely on geographical location as an alternative to CIDR assignment, but that implies either making the Internet topology sufficiently congruent to the geography, in which case the driving forces behind such a topology need to be understood, or accepting that the addresses are not topologically significant, in which case techniques other than hierarchical routing have to be developed.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses work like street addresses grouped by town, so the routers need few rules. The cost is that if you move to a provider in another town, every address you own has to change, and tools for doing that quickly were still rare.

sections.title: Information Sharing, Further Work and Conclusions
sections.content:
Ensuring Internet-wide coordination may become harder as the Internet grows, but stability and consistency of Internet-wide routing could benefit if the information about the routing requirements of various organisations were shared across organisational boundaries. Such information could be used in many situations, from troubleshooting to detecting and eliminating conflicting routing requirements. The scale of the Internet implies the information should be distributed, and the memo reports that work was underway to establish depositories of this information, called Routing Registries, as well as tools that analyse and use it.

The summary lists the issues the IAB thinks should be brought to the attention of the community. Two tasks require the most immediate attention: further work to develop technologies that facilitate renumbering, and further work to investigate the feasibility of routing information aggregation above the direct provider level. Three tasks are viewed as medium term: understanding the relative practical importance of the various routing requirements, understanding how those requirements affect the scalability of the routing system, and investigating alternatives to hierarchical routing. Four are viewed as long term: understanding and using the benefits of routing information sharing, understanding the implications of the virtual overlays created by encapsulation, understanding how different price structures influence routing requirements, and understanding how to balance the providers' goals against the public interest of Internet-wide connectivity and subscribers' choices.

The conclusions note that routing-related areas are not covered in the document, for instance multicast routing, routing in the presence of mobile hosts, and routing in the presence of a large shared medium such as ATM, and that further work is needed on those. The impact of a multi-provider Internet goes well beyond routing and reaches into network management and troubleshooting, and the memo says further work is needed to assess those implications and to understand how all these areas interact from a system-wide perspective. The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: If the network owners shared their rules with each other, fixing problems would be easier. The memo ends with a to-do list, the most urgent items first, and says security is not discussed.
